current.context: A flaw was found in libtirpc. The SunRPC UDP/datagram server transport reuses a single receive buffer across requests and resets the XDR decode position without rebinding the decode length to the size of the datagram actually received. As a result, when a short UDP RPC request is received after a longer one, the XDR decoder can read stale bytes left in the reused buffer and interpret them as part of the current request, including credential, verifier, or procedure-argument fields. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to data confidentiality and integrity for services that use a UDP-based SunRPC server.

current.context: The WP STAGING and WP STAGING Pro plugins for WordPress are vulnerable to PHP Object Injection in all versions up to, and including, 4.17.0 and 6.17.0, respectively, via deserialization of untrusted input during database restore and staging reset. This is due to the database importer treating attacker-controlled text beginning with {WPSTG_BINARY} as trusted internal binary data and decoding its hexadecimal suffix into serialized bytes. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with Subscriber-level access and above, to plant a malicious serialized object in their own profile. When an Administrator later performs an ordinary database-including restore or staging reset containing that value, and the restored profile metadata is loaded, either during the restore or in a later request, a built-in POP chain can be used to execute arbitrary code on the server. Additional built-in gadget chains allow arbitrary local file read in both WP STAGING and WP STAGING Pro and arbitrary file deletion in WP STAGING Pro. The attacker does not require Administrator credentials or a copy of a backup, but exploitation does require the later privileged restore or reset.

current.context: The AIKTP plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authorization Bypass via Predictable Token in all versions up to, and including, 5.0.7. The vulnerability exists because the plugin's sync token (`aiktpz_token`) is generated using PHP's non-cryptographic `uniqid()` function — producing a wall-clock-derived value with approximately one million microsecond candidates per uncertain generation second — while the unauthenticated, unthrottled REST endpoint `/wp-json/aiktp/checkToken` (registered with `permission_callback => __return_true`) acts as a public brute-force oracle for the token; simultaneously, the capability checks in `check_valid_token` and its wrappers (`verify_aiktp_token_with_edit_capability`, `verify_aiktp_token_with_upload_capability`) inspect only a server-side stored Administrator account (option `aiktp_author`) rather than the actual REST caller, meaning possession of the token alone grants Administrator-equivalent authority to any external request. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to recover the sync token and then invoke `POST /wp-json/aiktp/createpost` to publish arbitrary posts attributed to a site Administrator, `POST /wp-json/aiktp/doUpdatePostWithImageURL` to overwrite the body content of any existing post, and `POST /wp-json/aiktp/doUploadImageToWP` to import remote media and attach it as the featured image of any post. Additionally, when the `aiktpz_token` option has never been initialized, the `checkToken` oracle returns success for an empty token submission due to a loose comparison in `check_valid_token`, providing a zero-effort bypass that requires no brute-forcing whatsoever.

Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity vulnerability in benoitc idna allows an attacker who controls a hostname passed to the library to exhaust CPU via an over-long xn-- label. idna:ulabel/1 in src/idna.erl hands every ASCII label that starts with xn-- to punycode:decode/1 without applying check_label_length/1, the 63-octet DNS label limit. punycode:decode/1 in src/punycode.erl builds its output with list appends in insert/4, so its cost grows super-linearly with the label length. A label of a few kilobytes keeps a scheduler busy for seconds to minutes before the label is rejected as invalid punycode.

Every decode entry point reaches this path: decode/1, decode/2, to_unicode/1 and from_ascii/1. The encode path reaches it as well, because alabel/1 calls ulabel/1 on an ASCII xn-- label before its own length check, so encode/1, encode/2 and to_ascii/1 are affected for such input.

This issue affects idna: from 0.5.0 before 8.0.0.

current.context: The Masteriyo LMS – LMS Course Builder, Quizzes & Certificates plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to PHP Object Injection in versions up to, and including, 3.5.1 via deserialization of untrusted input in the course importer. The set_post_metas() method  calls maybe_unserialize() on attacker-controlled postmeta string values parsed from the uploaded JSON import file. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary PHP Objects. Exploitation by unauthenticated attackers requires that the site has enable_instructor_registration=true AND enable_guest_checkout=true AND at least one purchasable course exists. Install.php sets enable_instructor_registration=false on fresh installs, so this is a non-default configuration. On a default installation, where that is not configured, the vulnerability requires attackers with author-level access and above.

current.context: A flaw was found in OpenSCAP. This vulnerability allows for information disclosure when performing offline scans of untrusted filesystem images, such as container images or virtual machine (VM) disks. Because the scanner does not properly restrict symbolic link (symlink) resolution to the target image's root directory, an attacker can supply a crafted image containing links pointing to files on the host system. When the scan runs, typically with elevated privileges, OpenSCAP follows these links to read sensitive host files and expose their contents in the scan report or manipulate compliance results.

current.context: The Magic Login Mail or QR Code plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Privilege Escalation via Administrator Account Takeover in versions up to, and including, 2.07. This is due to the `curpageurl()` function falling back to the raw `$_SERVER['HTTP_HOST']` value — with no validation against the site's configured origin via `home_url()` or `site_url()` — when `get_the_permalink()` returns empty or false, allowing an attacker-controlled Host header to become the URL origin of the magic-login link generated by `generate_url()` and delivered to the target via `wp_mail()`. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to intercept the one-time uid and token pair sent to a targeted Administrator's email and replay them against the real site, causing `autologin_via_url()` to call `wp_set_auth_cookie()` and establish a full Administrator session on the targeted account. Exploitation requires the `[magic_login]` shortcode to render on a path where `get_the_permalink()` returns empty or false (such as a 404 page or a block-theme header template part), the web server to forward non-canonical Host headers, the attacker to know the target administrator's email address, and the administrator to click the attacker-originated magic-login link. Successful exploitation gives the attacker control of a distinct, already-privileged Administrator account; it does not promote the attacker's original account. Successful exploitation additionally requires an action by an administrator — the attacker cannot trigger the vulnerability on their own.

current.context: A flaw was found in ansible-builder. The regular expression used to strip comments from a collection's requirements.txt during introspection is susceptible to super-quadratic backtracking. A requirements file containing a line with a long run of internal whitespace and no comment character causes the comment-stripping routine to consume CPU time proportional to the square of the line length. An attacker who can get a victim to build an execution environment that includes an attacker-supplied collection can cause the ansible-builder build or introspect process to hang, resulting in a denial of service. This issue has no confidentiality or integrity impact.

current.context: A flaw was found in the Ansible language server shipped with the vscode-ansible extension. The regular expression used to extract documentation fragments from Ansible module files is susceptible to quadratic-time scanning. This issue has no confidentiality or integrity impact.

current.context: A double free in the X.509 name constraints enforcement of GnuTLS 3.8.13 on all platforms allows a remote attacker to cause a denial of service (application crash) via a certificate chain containing a NameConstraints extension processed while the application is under memory pressure. An authenticated user who can update a database password can trigger command substitution before the database command runs, resulting in arbitrary operating-system command execution with the Dokploy process privileges, which are typically root. This issue is fixed in version 0.31.1.

current.context: Dokploy is a free, self-hostable Platform as a Service (PaaS). Prior to 0.31.1, the Nixpacks publishDirectory build setting accepts shell metacharacters and is interpolated into a docker cp command executed through child_process.exec. An authenticated user with access to an application can execute arbitrary commands on the Dokploy host when triggering a Nixpacks deployment, leading to host compromise through the privileged Docker environment. This issue is fixed in version 0.31.1.

current.context: Dokploy is a free, self-hostable Platform as a Service (PaaS). Prior to 0.31.0, failed Railpack builds and database backups propagate an execution error containing the full command, exposing application environment variables, database passwords, and S3 access keys embedded in those commands. When the corresponding App Build Error or Database Backup notification setting is enabled, the disclosure can send secrets to email, Slack, Discord, Telegram, or webhooks; the same secrets are written separately to persistent Dokploy container logs, which may be accessible to more principals than the affected service. This issue is fixed in version 0.31.0.

current.context: k8s-mcp-server manages Kubernetes clusters through the Model Context Protocol. Prior to 1.1.0, SERVER_MODE defaults to SSE, with the listener on 0.0.0.0:8080, but main.go creates the SSE server without an authentication option or context function. The GET /sse handler creates a sessionId that is only a correlation value, and the POST /message handler accepts a loadable sessionId without an authorization or Origin check before dispatching tools/call; consequently, any client able to reach the port can enumerate and invoke registered Kubernetes tools without credentials. Read-only mode is disabled by default, leaving write-capable Kubernetes tools available to run with the server's configured cluster privileges. This issue is fixed in version 1.1.0.

current.context: sqlite-mcp is a Model Context Protocol server for SQLite. Prior to 0.1.2, the default read-only mode can be bypassed through execute_query, which accepts a leading SELECT while the SQLite driver executes trailing statements, and through describe_table, which interpolates the caller-controlled table_name into PRAGMA table_info. Either path can issue ATTACH DATABASE, which opens an attached file read-write despite mode=ro and can make the protected database writable, read other SQLite database files, or create a SQLite-format file at a path writable by the server process. Existing non-empty files that are not SQLite databases are refused and left unchanged. The server has no built-in authentication and listens on all interfaces at :8080 by default, so any client that can reach the port can invoke these tools unless an authenticating proxy is in place. This issue is fixed in version 0.1.2.

current.context: A caller who can send requests to the temporal-proxy gRPC listener can obtain the static API key of an upstream whose address is templated from the request namespace, and then use that key directly against the upstream Temporal service. temporal-proxy does not validate the request namespace before rendering it into a templated upstream address, so when an upstream's hostPort is templated from the namespace, as in the published Temporal Cloud configuration example, a crafted namespace changes the host the proxy dials. If that upstream verifies TLS against the system trust store and sets no literal server name, a caller-controlled host with a publicly trusted certificate passes verification and receives the key. The built-in static-token and JWKS authenticators do not restrict namespaces, so any caller they admit can do this; an external authenticator that admits only listed namespaces prevents it. temporal-proxy versions 0.1.0 through 1.2.0 are affected. The issue is fixed in 1.0.2, 1.1.2, and 1.2.1, and releases before 1.0.0 receive no fix. Upgrade to the fixed release for the deployed minor release line, and rotate any upstream API key that untrusted callers could reach.

current.context: When two templated upstreams in temporal-proxy render the same address, a request routed to one upstream can be sent under the other upstream's credential, namespace translation, and payload encryption keys. temporal-proxy pools connections for templated upstreams by rendered address and TLS server name only, although each upstream's outbound credential, namespace translation, and payload encryption keys, where configured, are attached to its connection. A request routed to one upstream can therefore be sent over the connection the other created, and the upstream Temporal service authorizes it as the other upstream's principal. Configuration validation rejects only identical hostPort values, so templates that differ in text but render the same address are accepted. This mixes the two upstreams' ordinary traffic, and a caller that an external authenticator restricts to one upstream's namespaces can use it to act under the other upstream's credential. Deployments with at most one templated upstream are not affected. temporal-proxy versions 0.1.0 through 1.1.1 are affected. The issue is fixed in 1.0.2, 1.1.2, and 1.2.0, and releases before 1.0.0 receive no fix. Upgrade to the fixed release for the deployed minor release line.

current.context: A caller with write permission in a namespace can terminate temporal-proxy through memory exhaustion by storing highly compressed payloads in Workflow history, and the stored history causes the same failure on every later read. temporal-proxy 1.2.0 decompresses every payload marked as compressed in the responses it forwards, whether or not compression is configured. Each payload is limited to 4 MiB after decompression, but the total for a response is not, and the decoded payloads are held in memory together. The caller can store many small, highly compressed payloads through the proxy or directly at the upstream Temporal service. When that history is read through the proxy, for example by a Worker processing a task, the proxy can run out of memory and be terminated. The codec server's /decode endpoint is affected in the same way when it is enabled. Only temporal-proxy 1.2.0 is affected; earlier versions do not decompress payloads. The issue is fixed in 1.2.1. Upgrade to 1.2.1 or later.

current.context: A caller who can reach the temporal-proxy gRPC listener, with or without a valid credential, can grow the proxy's memory until the process is terminated by sending requests with many distinct gRPC method names. temporal-proxy labels its request metrics with the method name exactly as the caller sent it, and records every request, including those that authentication or routing reject. Each distinct method name adds metric series that are never removed. The series grow whether or not the metrics endpoint is scraped, and metric labels configured from request metadata multiply the growth. temporal-proxy versions 0.1.0-alpha.20260716 through 1.2.0 are affected. The issue is fixed in 1.0.2, 1.1.2, and 1.2.1, and releases before 1.0.0 receive no fix. Upgrade to the fixed release for the deployed minor release line.

current.context: Zyrabit Platform provides sovereign AI infrastructure for enterprise retrieval-augmented generation. Prior to 2.4.4, import_to_vault(source_path, destination_name) accepts both caller-controlled paths, but the content-pattern guard does not confine destination_name. The vulnerable tool is implemented in zyrabit-slm/api-rag/app/domain/services/mcp_service.py, where Path(DOCS_DIR) / destination_name is passed to shutil.copy2, allowing traversal or an absolute destination to write outside the vault. An unrestricted source_path can be copied into the vault and retrieved through secure_query, disclosing files readable by the service; files that do not match the executable-pattern filter pass that filter. When ENABLE_LEGACY_EXTENSIONS=true, zyrabit-slm/api-rag/app/main.py registers POST /mcp/rpc without get_current_user, allowing unauthenticated network tool calls; this optional exposure is disabled by default and is not required for local invocation. If an attacker can stage chosen source content and write to an execution-triggered destination, the advisory describes conditional process execution. This issue is fixed in version 2.4.4.

current.context: Bazarr is a companion application to Sonarr and Radarr. Prior to 1.6.3-beta.11, the /api/subtitles/subtitles-info handler uses SubtitleNameContents.get() in subtitles_contents.py and reads the caller-supplied subtitlePath after checking only its subtitle extension; because the resolved path is not confined to files indexed by Bazarr, traversal can read files outside the media library. The /api/subtitles/subtitles handler in subtitles.py passes caller-supplied path and reference to sync and translation without per-path authorization, allowing an out-of-library reference file to be read and output to overwrite a file outside the media library. The authenticate decorator gates both endpoints when API authentication is enabled, while auth = None allows access without credentials. Both paths can affect only files that the Bazarr process can read or write. This issue is fixed in version 1.6.3-beta.11.

current.context: In Eclipse Yasson versions 3.0 to 3.0.5, a race condition (CWE-362) exists in the handling of @JsonbNumberFormat. Yasson creates one java.text.NumberFormat instance per annotated property and shares it across all threads that use the same Jsonb instance. NumberFormat is not thread-safe, and the deserializer called parse() on it without synchronization. When multiple threads deserialize concurrently, a thread can receive a numeric value that belongs to another thread's input, receive an incorrect value, or fail with an exception. A remote attacker who can send concurrent requests to an application that deserializes untrusted JSON this way may cause incorrect data to be processed or cause another user's value to be returned. Exploitation requires that the application use @JsonbNumberFormat with a shared Jsonb instance and that the attacker win a timing race. This issue is fixed in version 3.0.6 by synchronizing access to the shared NumberFormat instances.

current.context: MISP contains an authorization flaw in the user login-email change logic. When an external authentication backend is configured (LDAP, Shibboleth, ApacheSecureAuth, or CustomAuth), the login email address serves as the key by which the directory service resolves a user's identity, organization, and role on each login. The __canChangeLogin() method in UsersController only checked the MISP.disable_user_login_change setting and site-admin status; it did not account for whether an external authentication backend was active. As a result, any authenticated non-admin user (including org admins) could change their own login email to an address that matches a higher-privilege account in the external directory. On the user's next login, the external backend would resolve that email to the target directory identity, granting the attacker the organization and role associated with that identity. This constitutes an account-identity capture and privilege escalation: the attacker effectively assumes the identity of any directory account whose email they can guess or discover. The vulnerability requires an authenticated session with a valid API key or session token and a MISP instance configured with at least one external authentication backend. The impact is limited to the scope of the captured directory identity's privileges within MISP.

nvd.description: MISP contains an authorization flaw in the user login-email change logic. When an external authentication backend is configured (LDAP, Shibboleth, ApacheSecureAuth, or CustomAuth), the login email address serves as the key by which the directory service resolves a user's identity, organization, and role on each login. The __canChangeLogin() method in UsersController only checked the MISP.disable_user_login_change setting and site-admin status; it did not account for whether an external authentication backend was active. As a result, any authenticated non-admin user (including org admins) could change their own login email to an address that matches a higher-privilege account in the external directory. On the user's next login, the external backend would resolve that email to the target directory identity, granting the attacker the organization and role associated with that identity. This constitutes an account-identity capture and privilege escalation: the attacker effectively assumes the identity of any directory account whose email they can guess or discover. The vulnerability requires an authenticated session with a valid API key or session token and a MISP instance configured with at least one external authentication backend. The impact is limited to the scope of the captured directory identity's privileges within MISP.

current.context: A flaw was found in the file-xmc plugin in GIMP. When processing a specially crafted XMC image file, the plugin does not properly validate the comment subtype before using it as an array index. This missing validation leads to out-of-bounds memory access, invalid free and use-after-free issues. This vulnerability can result in an application crash, leading to a denial of service, or potentially allow for arbitrary code execution.

current.context: When payload encryption is enabled, failure messages and stack traces that temporal-proxy is configured to keep from the upstream Temporal service can reach it in plaintext, where anyone who can read the Workflow's history at the upstream can read them. When the proxy returns a failure to a Worker, it decrypts the failure's encoded attributes and copies the message and stack trace back onto the failure, keeping the attributes. A Worker that sends that failure back through the proxy, as SDKs do when an Activity failure becomes the cause of a Workflow failure, sends the restored text with it, and the proxy forwards the text unchanged because the failure already has encoded attributes. The upstream then stores the text in plaintext beside its encrypted copy. This affects deployments that enable failure encryption in the proxy, and deployments that leave it off while the SDK encodes failure attributes itself. Payloads are not affected. temporal-proxy versions 0.9.0 through 1.2.0 are affected. The issue is fixed in 1.0.2, 1.1.2, and 1.2.1, and releases before 1.0.0 receive no fix. Upgrade to the fixed release for the deployed minor release line.

current.context:
MISP contains an authorization bypass in its event search and filter functionality. When a user performed searches through events/restSearch (value, value prefix, searchall, type, uuid, attribute tags, object filters), objects/restSearch, or the event index tag, galaxy, and quick filters, the underlying SQL subqueries matched against attributes and objects without enforcing the per-attribute distribution, sharing-group, or soft-deleted visibility rules that apply when fetching individual elements.

A user who could view an event (for example, a community-distributed event) could therefore use search to determine whether organisation-only, sharing-group-restricted, or soft-deleted attributes and objects existed within that event. Because the value filter supports prefix matching (LIKE), an attacker could enumerate the full value of a hidden attribute one character at a time. Tags attached exclusively to hidden attributes also leaked through the tag, galaxy, and quick-filter paths on the event index.

The vulnerability affects the EventsController quick-filter and index-filter logic, the Event model wildcard/value/uuid/tag filter methods, the MispAttribute tag filter, the MispObject buildFilterConditions and restSearch methods, and the ReportFromEvent object filter. Site administrators and users belonging to the event's own organisation retain full visibility, and sync users continue to match soft-deleted elements as intended.

The issue was reported by ENISA.

current.context: MISP contains an authorization bypass in the correlations/eventCorrelations endpoint and the underlying correlation engines (Default and OnDemand). The CorrelationsController::eventCorrelations action did not verify that the requesting user was permitted to view the event specified by the event ID parameter. Any authenticated user could supply the ID of an event belonging to another organisation (distribution level 0, organisation-only) and receive its full correlation results, including attribute identifiers and values. Additionally, for events the user could partially view, the correlation engines filtered only the related (target) side of each correlation row and did not vet the queried event's own source attributes. As a result, correlations keyed by attributes hidden from the user (organisation-only attributes, attributes in sharing groups the user is not a member of, or attributes inside organisation-only objects) were returned with their IDs and values. The Default engine's related-event listing (used in events/view) also included events related solely through such hidden attributes. The vulnerability was reported by ENISA. Successful exploitation requires a valid authenticated session with any role and knowledge or enumeration of a target event ID. The security impact is disclosure of threat-intelligence attribute values (IP addresses, domain names, etc.) and attribute identifiers that the user is not authorised to see, as well as confirmation of the existence of otherwise invisible events.

current.context: MISP's EventDelegationsController delegateEvent method accepted a user-supplied sharing_group_id parameter without verifying that the requesting user was a member of the referenced sharing group. When a delegation request was submitted with distribution set to 4 (sharing-group distribution), the raw sharing_group_id value was stored directly into the EventDelegation record. The delegation view subsequently rendered the stored sharing group's name back to the requester. Because no authorization check was performed, any authenticated user with delegation permission could enumerate sharing group identifiers (by guessing sequential IDs or other values) and read the names of sharing groups to which their organisation did not belong, including hidden or restricted groups. Hidden, missing, and malformed identifiers were not distinguished in the response, but the successful case still leaked the group name. The vulnerability required an authenticated session with the perm_delegate capability and knowledge of a valid event ID to delegate. The security impact is limited to disclosure of sharing group names (a low-impact confidentiality breach) and does not grant access to the group's contents or modify any data.

current.context: MISP contains an access control flaw in its tag management endpoints: events/addTag (single and bulk), events/removeTag, and attributes/removeTag. These endpoints loaded their target event or attribute using an unscoped database query (recursive = -1) that did not apply the calling user's ACL visibility rules. As a result, two distinct security issues existed: (1) Information disclosure: the removeTag endpoint returned different responses depending on whether a given tag was present on a hidden event, allowing an authenticated user to enumerate which tags were applied to events they had no visibility into. (2) Unauthorized modification: users belonging to the host organisation, who are permitted to set local tags on records they can see, could add or remove local tags on events and attributes they could not see, because the canModifyTag ACL check operated on the unscoped object without first verifying the caller's visibility. The fix replaces the unscoped find() calls with ACL-aware fetch methods (fetchSimpleEvent and fetchAttributeSimple) that apply the user's visibility before the object is returned, and adds an explicit empty-object check in removeTag so that a hidden event responds identically to a non-existent one. Affected components include the EventsController (addTag, removeTag), the AttributesController (removeTag), and the ACLComponent (canModifyTag). The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with at least the tagger role (perm_tagger) or host-organisation membership.

current.context: MISP contains an information disclosure vulnerability in the Sighting model when the Sightings_anonymise setting is enabled. The listSightings and sightings/restSearch endpoints accepted a caller-supplied org_id filter parameter and applied it directly to the SQL query without verifying whether the requesting user was authorized to filter by that organisation. Because the anonymization mechanism masks the reporter's organisation in the returned records, a non-site-admin user could bypass the anonymization by specifying another organisation's ID in the filter. The query would then return only that organisation's sightings, effectively naming the reporter and defeating the purpose of the anonymization feature. A negated filter (NOT IN) similarly revealed which sightings belonged to the target organisation by exclusion. The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with sighting read permissions (perm_sighting) who is not a site administrator, and the Sightings_anonymise plugin setting must be enabled. The security impact is the disclosure of which organisation reported a given sighting, undermining the privacy guarantees that the anonymization feature is designed to provide. This issue was reported by ENISA.

current.context:
MISP contains an authorization flaw in the GalaxyCluster model's captureCluster() function, which handles the import and synchronization of Galaxy Clusters. Prior to the fix, any authenticated user holding the galaxy editor role could replace an existing locked Galaxy Cluster by supplying its UUID in an import request, regardless of which organization owned the cluster. The function unconditionally called captureOrganisationAndSG() before the save operation, overwriting the cluster's org_id and orgc_id fields with the importing user's organization, effectively transferring ownership of the cluster to the attacker's organization. Additionally, the save operation was not restricted to a specific set of fields, allowing arbitrary field modification.

The vulnerable behavior required the attacker to possess a valid MISP account with the perm_galaxy_editor role and to know or discover the UUID of a target cluster belonging to another organization. No site-admin or owner-organization privilege was enforced for the update path. The result was that a low-privilege galaxy editor in one organization could modify the content (value, description, distribution, etc.) of clusters owned by other organizations and seize ownership, corrupting the integrity of shared threat-intelligence data across the MISP instance.

The vulnerability was reported by ENISA and CERT.pl. The fix introduces an explicit authorization gate that restricts cluster updates to the owner organization, a sync user who can see the cluster via sharing-group rules, or a site administrator, and enforces a field allow-list that excludes org_id and orgc_id from update writes, preserving original ownership.

current.context: MISP contains an authorization bypass vulnerability in the Galaxy import/sync functionality (captureGalaxy in app/Model/Galaxy.php). The captureGalaxy() method matched an incoming galaxy payload to an existing galaxy by UUID and unconditionally overwrote the matched record, regardless of whether the importing user belonged to the owning organization or whether the galaxy was a system-provided default galaxy. Any authenticated user holding the perm_galaxy_editor role could therefore: (1) demote a default galaxy by setting its default flag to false, (2) reassign the galaxy's org_id and orgc_id to the attacker's organization, effectively taking ownership, and (3) modify other galaxy fields (name, description, distribution, version). Additionally, the role-level permission check (perm_site_admin or perm_galaxy_editor) was executed after the captureOrganisationAndSG() call, meaning organization and sharing-group data was already captured before the authorization decision was made. The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with the perm_galaxy_editor role and the ability to submit a galaxy import payload containing a UUID that matches an existing galaxy. The security impact is loss of data integrity across the MISP instance: default galaxy definitions are corrupted, cross-organization ownership is silently transferred, and the integrity of shared threat-intelligence galaxy metadata is compromised for all users of the instance.

current.context: The WP Duplicate – WordPress Migration Plugin plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Directory Traversal in all versions up to, and including, 1.1.11 via the 'file_name' parameter. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to read the contents of arbitrary files on the server, which can contain sensitive information. The authentication bypass requires submitting the JSON boolean `true` as the `prod_key_random_id` value, which coerces against any non-empty stored secret so that the loose `!=` comparison evaluates to false, skipping the rejection branch entirely without knowledge of the secret.

This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to read the contents of arbitrary files on the server, which can contain sensitive information. The authentication bypass requires submitting the JSON boolean `true` as the `prod_key_random_id` value, which coerces against any non-empty stored secret so that the loose `!=` comparison evaluates to false, skipping the rejection branch entirely without knowledge of the secret.

current.context: The WP Duplicate – WordPress Migration Plugin plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Remote Code Execution in all versions up to, and including, 1.1.11 via the save_single_batch_file function. This is due to a PHP type-juggling authentication bypass via loose != comparison with no is_string() guard, combined with unsanitized base64-decoded path construction in save_single_batch_file() lacking any directory traversal containment. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with custom-level access and above, to execute code on the server. Exploitation requires that the site owner has completed the plugin's initial setup so that the site_type and prod_key_random_id options are non-empty, though any non-empty secret value is bypassable via the type-juggling flaw.

current.context:
Cross-site scripting in the embedded co-browsing feature in Unblu inc. Unblu Spark 7.0 through 7.57.9 and 8.0 before 8.40.2, on on-premises and cloud deployments, allows an unauthenticated remote attacker in the visitor role to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the browser of an agent taking part in the attacker's co-browsing session, via manipulated synchronized page attributes of the co-browsed page.



The JavaScript runs in the context and under the identity of the agent's session in the Agent Desk or the Single Conversation Desk.



Exploitation requires an agent to join an embedded co-browsing session with the attacker. Mobile co-apping isn't affected.

current.context: Chamilo LMS is an open-source learning management system. Prior to 1.11.40 and 2.0.1, main/lp/lp_ajax_save_objectives.php and public/main/lp/lp_ajax_save_objectives.php trust the request uid parameter instead of the authenticated user identity when saving SCORM learning objectives. Any authenticated student can replace uid with another user's identifier and overwrite that user's objectives because the endpoint performs no ownership check. This issue is fixed in versions 1.11.40 and 2.0.1.

current.context: mini-snmpd is a minimal SNMP agent implementation. Prior to 1.7, the ASN.1 BER parser in protocol.c does not verify that an attacker-controlled field length is no greater than the remaining packet size before decode_str(), decode_oid(), and decode_ptr() evaluate size - len + 1. When len exceeds size, unsigned size_t arithmetic wraps and bypasses the bounds check, allowing the decoder to read beyond the 2048-byte packet buffer. Parsing occurs before the SNMP community string is checked, so a remote unauthenticated attacker can send one crafted request to UDP port 161 to crash the process and potentially disclose adjacent heap memory. This issue is fixed in version 1.7.

current.context: djangocms-versioning is a general-purpose versioning package for django CMS 4 and later. Prior to 2.6.1, the check_discard and check_edit_redirect Conditions on djangocms_versioning.models.Version omit user_can_change, while VersionAdmin.discard_view and VersionAdmin.edit_redirect_view obtain a version by its primary key and rely on those conditions for object-level authorization. current.context: Music Assistant is an open-source media library manager that integrates streaming services with connected speakers. current.context: OliveTin gives safe and simple access to predefined shell commands from a web interface. From 3000.0.0 until 3000.18.1, OliveTin passes attacker-influenceable output and ot_username values into shellAfterCompleted processing in service/internal/executor/executor.go without applying checkShellArgumentSafety, the shell-safety validation used for primary action execution. current.context: DOMShell is a Chrome automation project whose MCP server exposes Unix-style tools for AI agents. Prior to 2.0.8, the DOMShell MCP server classifies the domshell_eval tool and eval command as read-tier operations that can run without --allow-write, even though eval shares the Runtime.evaluate dispatch path with the write-tier js command and has no side-effect gate. An MCP caller with tool-session access can therefore use domshell_eval to mutate DOM, window, or global state while the host approval interface, server authorization flags, denial messages, and audit records represent the operation as read-only. The bypass does not expose a capability beyond domshell_js for callers already authorized to write, but it violates the configured permission boundary for callers lacking that authorization. This issue is fixed in version 2.0.8.

current.context: Miren Runtime provides the runtime component for the Miren application platform. Prior to 0.11.1, the QUIC/HTTP3 RPC server on the default port 8443 uses tls.RequestClientCert and does not verify that presented certificates chain to the configured cluster certificate authority. The RPC authenticators derive a caller identity from PeerCertificates[0].Subject.CommonName without requiring a non-empty VerifiedChains value, and certificate identities bypass all RBAC checks. A network attacker who can reach the listener can present a self-signed certificate with an issuer distinguished name matching the public cluster CA subject and gain cluster superuser access, allowing disclosure, modification, or disruption of applications, sandboxes, disks, credentials, and other managed resources. This issue is fixed in version 0.11.1.

current.context: OpenID4VP is an open-source credential parsing library for SD-JWT VC and mDOC/mDL formats. Prior to 0.8.1, src/trust/ChainBuilder.ts ChainBuilder.tryBuild() terminates chain construction when an attacker-controlled certificate Subject Distinguished Name equals a trusted anchor subject, without verifying cryptographic closure to the anchor public key. A remote unauthenticated attacker can supply a self-signed leaf or intermediate that reuses the trusted Subject Distinguished Name and have credentials signed by the attacker key accepted as issued by the trusted authority. The public src/trust/TrustEvaluator.ts TrustEvaluator.evaluate() path compounds the error by matching a terminus through serialNumber and falling back to anchors[0], which can attribute the forged chain to genuine trusted-authority metadata. This issue is fixed in version 0.8.1.

current.context: PGPainless is a simple-to-use OpenPGP API based on Bouncy Castle. Prior to 1.7.8 and from 2.0.0 until 2.0.4, pgpainless-sop/src/main/kotlin/org/pgpainless/sop/InlineDetachImpl.kt InlineDetachImpl and pgpainless-core/src/main/kotlin/org/pgpainless/decryption_verification/MessageInspector.kt MessageInspector manually descend PGPCompressedData packets without incrementing or enforcing MAX_LAYER_DEPTH. A remote unauthenticated attacker can supply an untrusted OpenPGP message containing deeply nested compressed packet structures to a downstream application using inline-detach or message inspection, bypass the intended 16-layer limit, and force continued decompression and packet processing. The resulting resource consumption can block processing threads, exhaust heap memory, and crash the consuming application. This issue is fixed in versions 1.7.8 and 2.0.4.

current.context: keystore-go is a Go implementation of the Java KeyStore encoder and decoder. In 2.1.0 and earlier, keystore.Decode in decoder.go does not check the error returned when reading the trailing SHA-1 integrity digest and bounds its comparison by the length of the digest actually read. If an attacker with write access removes the final 20-byte digest from a modified JKS file, the empty actual digest causes the comparison loop to execute zero times and Decode returns the parsed keystore without an error. For certificate-only stores using TrustedCertificateEntry values, this bypasses both tamper detection and password verification, allowing trusted CA certificates to be added or replaced without knowing the keystore password and potentially enabling interception or modification of TLS connections that trust the forged CA. This issue is fixed in version 3.0.0.

A successful exploit could allow the attacker to effectively cause the ClamAV to exceed the MaxFileSize and potentially get caught in an infinite loop, causing a DoS condition.

current.context: Todoist MCP Server provides tools that allow AI agents to access and modify a Todoist account. Prior to 10.3.3, the optional todoist-mcp-http server accepts browser-origin requests to POST /mcp without validating the Host and Origin headers or authenticating the browser caller. A malicious website can use DNS rebinding to reach the loopback listener and invoke MCP tools through StreamableHTTPServerTransport, which uses the server-held Todoist API key. This exposes Todoist account data and permits operations such as task creation, updates, completion, and deletion. The stdio transport is not browser-reachable and is not affected by this attack path. This issue is fixed in version 10.3.3.

current.context: Axon is an agent-agnostic context engine that gives AI coding agents continuous memory across sessions, tools, and machines. Prior to 0.1.1, rtk-install in src/axon/context/rtk_bootstrap.py uses _http_download() to fetch a prebuilt rtkx release archive and _extract_binary() to mark it executable, after which compress_text_with_rtk() invokes it without verifying a checksum, signature, or build attestation. If the sammyjdev/rtkx release pipeline or maintainer release credentials are compromised, an attacker can supply a modified binary that executes with the Axon process privileges when a user installs or automatically bootstraps rtkx. This issue is fixed in version 0.1.1.

current.context: NotrinosERP is an open-source web-based enterprise resource planning system written in PHP and MySQL. From 1.0.0 until 1.1.0, the employee document handler in hrm/manage/employees.php allows an authenticated user with SA_EMPLOYEE permission to submit doc_file through tab_documents() and stores the raw client filename, including an executable extension, under company/0/documents/employees/ without extension, MIME, or content validation. Uploading a PHP file places executable content beneath the web root, where requesting the stored file results in server-side code execution. This issue is fixed in version 1.1.0.

current.context: obsidian-sync-mcp is an MCP server that gives AI agents access to Obsidian vaults. Prior to 0.5.7, deployments running without MCP_AUTH_TOKEN install no serverOptions.authenticate check for the HTTP /mcp endpoint, so requests are dispatched without validating the Host or Origin headers. A malicious website visited by the operator can use DNS rebinding to reach loopback, LAN, VPN, or container-published addresses, or directly issue a cross-origin request to loopback, and invoke the MCP tool surface to read, create, overwrite, delete, or move vault notes. Deployments using MCP_AUTH_TOKEN are not affected because browsers do not attach the bearer token. This issue is fixed in version 0.5.7.

current.context: The WP Duplicate – WordPress Migration Plugin plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Missing Authorization in versions up to, and including, 1.1.11. This is due to a missing capability check and missing nonce check on the start_zip_creation, start_zip_download, local_sync_get_init_root_files, and local_sync_get_files_by_key AJAX actions in the start_zip_creation_dev() and sibling functions. current.context:
In Eclipse iceoryx-rs, versions 0.0.11 to 0.0.13 and 0.1.0 as well as on the latest main branch.



`SampleReceiver::<T>::take()` and `Sample::<T>::deref()` are safe functions that hand the caller a `&T` pointing at a chunk written by another iceoryx process, but the subscriber path neither requires `T: ShmSend` nor verifies that the received chunk is at least `size_of::<T>()` bytes / `align_of::<T>()`-aligned. A peer process that publishes an undersized chunk, or any chunk at all when the subscriber chose a pointer-bearing `T`, drives a `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` subscriber into out-of-bounds reads of adjacent shared-memory chunks or dereference of a publisher-controlled pointer.



Resolution:



It will not be fixed since this is a known limitation in iceoryx as it is the users responsibility to specify the same data type on sender and receiver side.



[iceoryx2](https://github.com/eclipse-iceoryx/iceoryx2) is the successor of iceoryx-rs where the API is designed to prevent this by default.



It is strongly recommended to migrate to iceoryx2 which is actively maintained and receives security support.



The iceoryx-rs package has officially reached End-of-life and will not receive any features, bugfixes or security fixes.

current.context:
tcp_pkt_linearize() in subsys/net/ip/tcp.c is used by th_get() whenever a received TCP header is not contiguous in a single net_buf. While pulling the header bytes out of the following fragments, the loop called net_buf_unref() on an emptied fragment without first detaching its frags pointer. net_buf_unref() walks the whole fragment list, so the payload buffers still linked behind that fragment were freed as well, and the stale pointer was then reinstalled into the packet as buf->frags, producing a use-after-free and a later double free during packet teardown. The same loop also advanced to second->frags unconditionally: when the fragment still held payload after the header remainder was pulled, it was spliced out of the packet without ever being unreferenced, permanently leaking that buffer and silently dropping the data it carried.

The defect is reached from tcp_recv() via th_get() on every received TCP segment, before connection lookup or any header validation, so a single unauthenticated segment that matches a listening socket is sufficient. An attacker only needs the TCP header to straddle a net_buf boundary, which they can arrange from off-link: IPv6 extension headers are accepted on receive and their length is added to the header offset by th_get(), so a Destination Options header of a suitable length places the TCP header across the boundary of the fixed-size receive buffers (CONFIG_NET_BUF_DATA_SIZE). Packet chains assembled from several sources - IPv4/IPv6 reassembly, 6LoWPAN/802.15.4 reassembly, tunnel or virtual interfaces that strip an outer header, or drivers producing scatter-gather chains - can additionally present a short interior fragment that the loop empties exactly, which is the case that frees the remainder of the packet while it is still in use.

The reliably reachable consequence is exhaustion of the receive buffer pool: each crafted segment leaks one net_buf from the fixed CONFIG_NET_BUF_RX_COUNT pool, the buffers are never reclaimed, and once the pool is empty the device can no longer receive network traffic until it is rebooted. Where a fragment is emptied exactly, the impact rises to memory corruption: freed pool buffers are written through by the remainder of the loop, their contents may be delivered to the application, and the packet is double-freed on teardown.

The fix saves and clears second->frags before the net_buf_unref() so only the emptied header fragment is released, and advances to the next fragment only when second->len == 0, keeping any fragment that still holds payload in the packet. This restores the detach-before-unref ownership pattern used elsewhere in the stack, for example in net_pkt_trim_buffer().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ipv6: raw: fix use-after-free in rawv6_send_hdrinc()

rawv6_send_hdrinc() caches the route before handing the skb to
l3mdev_ip6_out(). The VRF output path may replace skb->dst and release
the original route, leaving the cached pointer stale.

The function later dereferences that pointer for statistics accounting
and as the output device passed to NF_HOOK(). Its RCU read-side critical
section starts after l3mdev_ip6_out(), so it cannot prevent the old route
from being reclaimed in between.

Reload the route from the current skb destination after
l3mdev_ip6_out() returns.

KASAN reports a slab-use-after-free in rawv6_sendmsg(), with the route
allocated by ip6_dst_alloc(), freed by dst_destroy() from rcu_core(), and
the related RCU callback queued from vrf_l3_out().

previous.context:
Bludit is vulnerable to Path Traversal in the page deletion functionality. An authenticated user with the Author role can set the UUID field of their own page to contain path traversal sequences (.. and path separators), which are saved without proper validation. When the page is deleted, Pages::delete() passes the path constructed from this UUID to Filesystem::deleteRecursive() without verifying that it still points to an allowed directory, allowing the attacker to delete any files, even not belonging to them. Critically, it is possible to delete admin pages and render the site unusable.


Because vendor contact attempts were unsuccessful, the vulnerability has only been confirmed in version 3.22.0 but may also affect other versions.

The backend endpoint for adding online media (e.g. YouTube or Vimeo videos) accepted a target folder in the fallback storage (storage uid 0), which points to the public web root of the installation. File mount and permission checks are not applied to the fallback storage. As a result, any authenticated, low-privileged backend user, even without file mounts or module access, could create online media files with a partially controllable file name in the public web root.

In combination with TYPO3-CORE-SA-2026-027, this could be used to re-enable the installer on an already configured instance. The installer could then be used to create a new administrator and system maintainer account, which leads to remote code execution.

previous.context:
The installer (first installation wizard) could be re-enabled on an already configured instance by placing a file whose name starts with FIRST_INSTALL in the public web root or the project root. The installer then became accessible without authentication, allowing for example to change the database connection and to create a new administrator and system maintainer account, which leads to remote code execution. As demonstrated in TYPO3-CORE-SA-2026-026, such a file could be created by an authenticated, low-privileged backend user without any further permissions. Other ways of creating files in the web root, as well as leftover or restored marker files, could be abused in the same way.

With the fixed versions, the installer can no longer be re-enabled on an already configured instance by a marker file. A new internal setting $GLOBALS['TYPO3_CONF_VARS']['SYS']['isInstalling'] is stored in the system configuration and is only enabled while a new installation is running. Additionally, only the exact file names FIRST_INSTALL and FIRST_INSTALL.txt are accepted as marker files.

previous.context:
ImageMagick and GraphicsMagick use small modules, called "coders", to read each image format. When processing images, TYPO3 determined the coder from the file type detected by the file contents, as long as the detected mime-type started with image/. A file containing MVG (Magick Vector Graphics) instructions, uploaded with an image file extension like .png, was therefore processed with the MVG coder. MVG instructions can read local files into the processed image, which allows disclosing the contents of arbitrary files readable by the web server, for example configuration files containing credentials, through a publicly accessible processed image.

Exploiting this vulnerability requires a way to upload files without a mime-type check, for example a public form of the Form Framework using a FileUpload or ImageUpload element without configured allowedMimeTypes (see TYPO3-CORE-SA-2026-032), which allows exploitation by unauthenticated visitors. Additionally, ImageMagick must be used for image processing, and its default system configuration must allow the MVG coder.

Files uploaded through FileUpload or ImageUpload elements are stored in an unguessable sub-folder that remains the same for the whole form session. If storing an uploaded file failed, for example because of a file name exceeding the file system's length limit, the raw error message was shown to the frontend user disclosing the storage path including the unguessable folder name and the server's temporary upload directory. With this information, attackers could determine the public URL of files they upload through the form.

If a form allows uploading files that browsers can execute, such as HTML documents, this could lead to Cross-Site Scripting on web servers that do not apply the Content-Security-Policy recommended by TYPO3 to the form upload target folder. This vulnerability is known to be actively exploited.

previous.context: The cHash argument, which ensures that only URL arguments originally generated by TYPO3 create separate page cache entries, was treated inconsistently when it was passed as an array. The cHash validation treated such a value as missing, while the page cache identifier treated it as present and included all URL arguments. As a result, unauthenticated visitors could create an unlimited number of page cache entries and trigger uncached page renderings by adding an array cHash with arbitrary values to any URL. This could exhaust server resources and fill the page cache storage. Only installations where the cHash validation is not enforced via $GLOBALS['TYPO3_CONF_VARS']['FE']['cacheHash']['enforceValidation'] are affected. This setting is enabled by default for new installations since TYPO3 v12, but is often still disabled in installations upgraded from older versions.

previous.context: The FileUpload and ImageUpload elements of the Form Framework use the property allowedMimeTypes as an allow list of MIME types accepted for upload. An empty allowedMimeTypes list was treated as "no restriction". Forms containing upload elements without any configured MIME type, for example in manually created form definitions or when all MIME types were deselected in the form editor, accepted any file except those blocked by the file deny pattern, which only covers PHP-related file extensions. This allowed unauthenticated users to upload files with browser-executable content, such as HTML or SVG documents, to the configured upload folder, which by default is located in a public storage. If attackers know the URL of an uploaded file (see TYPO3-CORE-SA-2026-029), this could lead to Cross-Site Scripting on web servers that do not apply the Content-Security-Policy recommended by TYPO3 to the form upload target folder.

pretix provides a mechanism where ticket QR codes are cryptographically signed and can be verified by our pretixSCAN apps in offline mode without any database of valid tickets. pretixSCAN checks the signature to verify that the ticket was issued by the correct pretix event and compares the QR code against a list of revoked QR codes. A QR code becomes revoked when the order is canceled, or the ticket is changed in a way that a new QR code needs to be generated.




However, the parsing of the QR code in all of our pretixSCAN apps contained a faulty computation, rendering the check for the correct length of the contents faulty. This way, an attacker is able to craft multiple QR codes for the same ticket which have the same content, but look different and therefore do not match against the revocation list. This does not allow to fabricate entirely new tickets, but it does allow to enter the event with e.g. a canceled ticket. This attack requires pretixSCAN to be scanning in offline mode and the "pretix signature scheme 1" to be used for the event's QR codes.




If the attack is executed, the ticket unfortunately shows as valid (green) on the scanner but as invalid (red) on the server since the server later cannot match it to a ticket. We scanned the entire database of scans on pretix Hosted and could not find any traces of this being exploited in the past.

A QR code becomes revoked when the order is canceled, or the ticket is changed in a way that a new QR code needs to be generated.




However, the parsing of the QR code in all of our pretixSCAN apps contained a faulty computation, rendering the check for the correct length of the contents faulty. This way, an attacker is able to craft multiple QR codes for the same ticket which have the same content, but look different and therefore do not match against the revocation list. This does not allow to fabricate entirely new tickets, but it does allow to enter the event with e.g. a canceled ticket. This attack requires pretixSCAN to be scanning in offline mode and the "pretix signature scheme 1" to be used for the event's QR codes.




If the attack is executed, the ticket unfortunately shows as valid (green) on the scanner but as invalid (red) on the server since the server later cannot match it to a ticket. We scanned the entire database of scans on pretix Hosted and could not find any traces of this being exploited in the past.

Deserialization of Untrusted Data in Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code. The XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester.

This is the same vulnerability as CVE-2026-82384, which listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected. This issue is being actively exploited.

Users are recommended to upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later, which disables the extension types and rejects XML-RPC requests when the XML-RPC feature is disabled.

Users who cannot upgrade right away should set "enabledForExtensions" to "false" in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the "/roller-services/xmlrpc" servlet mapping, and restart Roller. Disabling XML-RPC in the administration UI is not enough, because older versions deserialize the request before checking that setting.

previous.context: The Vert.x HTTP client transport (a2a-java-sdk-http-client-vertx) hand-rolls a POST redirect follower that, when the documented PostBuilder.followRedirects(true) opt-in is enabled, re-issues the redirected request with the full request header map copied verbatim and performs no credential stripping and no same-authority check. A malicious, compromised, or mistyped agent that returns a 30x response with an absolute cross-host Location causes the client to forward the standard Authorization header (Bearer/Basic/OAuth) — plus every other header, including the allowlisted API-key headers — to the attacker-controlled authority. This breaks the project's own cross-transport invariant (SECURITY.md §8, OkHttpPostRedirectHeaderLeakTest) that credentials are stripped on cross-authority redirects even when redirects are followed. nvd.description: The Vert.x HTTP client transport (a2a-java-sdk-http-client-vertx) hand-rolls a POST redirect follower that, when the documented PostBuilder.followRedirects(true) opt-in is enabled, re-issues the redirected request with the full request header map copied verbatim and performs no credential stripping and no same-authority check. A malicious, compromised, or mistyped agent that returns a 30x response with an absolute cross-host Location causes the client to forward the standard Authorization header (Bearer/Basic/OAuth) — plus every other header, including the allowlisted API-key headers — to the attacker-controlled authority. This breaks the project's own cross-transport invariant (SECURITY.md §8, OkHttpPostRedirectHeaderLeakTest) that credentials are stripped on cross-authority redirects even when redirects are followed.
